title: Emergency Phrases in Spanish: What to Say When You Need Help
seo_title: Emergency Phrases in Spanish: What to Say When You Need Help
meta_description: Emergency phrases in Spanish for Americans: calling 911, helping a Spanish speaker, medical emergencies, accidents, theft and travel to Mexico or Spain.
excerpt: Short, clear phrases you hope you’ll never need, but should know.
body_html:
Emergency phrases in Spanish are the ones you hope never to use, but knowing them can make a real difference, whether you’re helping a Spanish-speaking neighbor here in the United States or traveling in Mexico, Latin America or Spain. In a stressful moment, long sentences disappear from your head, so this guide focuses on short, clear phrases you can say even when you’re frightened. At home, the number is always 911, and many 911 centers can connect you to a Spanish interpreter. Abroad, 911 also works in Mexico and much of Latin America, while Spain and the rest of Europe use 112.

Key takeaways
  • Shout for help: ¡Socorro! or ¡Ayuda!
  • In the US, Mexico and most of Latin America, call 911; in Spain, call 112.
  • Key phrase: Necesito ayuda. (I need help.)
  • Give your location first: Estoy en…
{{toc}}

Emergency phrases in Spanish: the essentials

SpanishEnglish
¡Socorro! / ¡Ayuda!Help!
Necesito ayuda.I need help.
¡Llame a una ambulancia!Call an ambulance!
¡Llame a la policía!Call the police!
¡Fuego!Fire!
Es una emergencia.It’s an emergency.
¿Habla inglés?Do you speak English?

In the US, the official 911 program explains how 911 centers work, including interpretation for callers who don’t speak English. If you travel, check the emergency number for your destination before you go: 911 in Mexico, Colombia, Argentina and many other countries, 112 in Spain.

Calling emergency services

When you call, the operator will ask what happened and where you are. Speak slowly and give the most important information first:

  • Hay un herido. Someone is injured.
  • Estoy en la calle Mayor, número 15. I’m at 15 Calle Mayor.
  • Estoy cerca de la estación / del hotel… I’m near the station / the hotel…
  • No sé dónde estoy. I don’t know where I am.
  • Mi número de teléfono es… My phone number is…
  • Hable más despacio, por favor. Please speak more slowly.

Operators in tourist areas often speak English; ask ¿Hay alguien que hable inglés? if you need to.

Medical emergencies

  • Se ha desmayado. He/she has fainted.
  • No respira. He/she isn’t breathing.
  • Está sangrando mucho. He/she is bleeding a lot.
  • Creo que es un infarto. I think it’s a heart attack.
  • Tiene una reacción alérgica. He/she is having an allergic reaction.
  • Es diabético/a. He/she is diabetic.
  • ¿Dónde está el hospital más cercano? Where is the nearest hospital?

For non-urgent health problems, see {{link:at-the-doctor-in-spanish|at the doctor in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Accidents

  • Ha habido un accidente. There’s been an accident.
  • Me he caído. I’ve fallen.
  • Creo que me he roto el brazo. I think I’ve broken my arm.
  • No puedo mover la pierna. I can’t move my leg.
  • ¿Está usted bien? Are you okay?

Theft and police

  • ¡Al ladrón! Stop, thief!
  • Me han robado la cartera / el celular. My wallet / phone has been stolen.
  • He perdido el pasaporte. I’ve lost my passport.
  • Quiero poner una denuncia. I want to report a crime.
  • ¿Dónde está la comisaría? Where is the police station?
  • Necesito contactar con la embajada de Estados Unidos. I need to contact the US embassy.

You will usually need a police report (la denuncia) for insurance claims and replacement documents.

Fire and natural events

  • ¡Hay un incendio! There’s a fire!
  • Llamen a los bomberos. Call the fire brigade.
  • ¿Dónde está la salida de emergencia? Where is the emergency exit?
  • ¡Salgan del edificio! Get out of the building!
  • Terremoto (earthquake), inundación (flood).

Getting lost or needing help

  • Me he perdido. I’m lost.
  • ¿Me puede ayudar? Can you help me?
  • He perdido a mi hijo/a. I’ve lost my child.
  • Tiene ocho años y lleva una camiseta roja. He/she is eight and is wearing a red T-shirt.

For directions in non-urgent situations, see {{link:polite-requests-in-spanish|polite requests in Spanish}}.

Practical tips before you travel

Save the local emergency number and the nearest US embassy or consulate in your contacts, and consider enrolling in the State Department’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) so the embassy can reach you. Keep a photo of your passport and insurance details on your phone. Learn your hotel’s address in Spanish, and write a short note in Spanish with any allergies or medical conditions, for example Soy alérgico a la penicilina, to show medical staff if you can’t speak. Many emergency services also offer text or app options for people who can’t talk. In a crisis, simple words are enough: Ayuda, por favor. Hay un herido. Estoy en… will get help on its way.

Helping a Spanish speaker in the US

Millions of people in the United States speak Spanish at home, so you may be the one who needs to help, at work, in your neighborhood or on the street. Simple phrases make a big difference: ¿Está bien? ¿Me oye? (Are you okay? Can you hear me?), No se mueva (Don’t move), Tranquilo/a, ya viene la ambulancia (Stay calm, the ambulance is coming), ¿Cómo se llama? (What’s your name?) and ¿Toma algún medicamento? (Do you take any medication?). If others are around, ask someone specific to call: Usted, llame al 112, por favor. Pointing at one person makes it much more likely that someone will actually make the call.

Useful words

urgencias (ER, emergency room), la ambulancia, los bomberos (fire brigade), la policía, el herido (injured person), la farmacia de guardia (on-duty pharmacy, open at night), el seguro (insurance) and la embajada (embassy). Knowing these few nouns helps you understand signs and instructions, even when you can’t follow every word someone says.

Final thoughts

Memorize ¡Socorro!, Necesito ayuda, Llame a una ambulancia and how to give your location. Save 112 or 911 in your phone. You’ll travel with more peace of mind. For everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you say “help” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¡Socorro! or ¡Ayuda! To ask directly: Necesito ayuda or ¿Me puede ayudar?

faq.q: What is the emergency number in Mexico and Spain?
faq.a: 911 in Mexico, as in the US and much of Latin America; 112 in Spain and the rest of the EU.

faq.q: How do I help a Spanish speaker call 911 in the US?
faq.a: Call 911 and say “Spanish, please” or ask for an interpreter. Many 911 centers can connect a Spanish interpreter to the call.
